source: U.S. National Park Service, 'War in the Coalfields: The Ludlow Massacre'

oneLiner: Senghenydd, Wales, 14 Oct 1913 — a firedamp blast killed 440 at Universal Colliery (60 under 20); manager Edward Shaw was fined £24, the press reckoned 'lives at 1/1¼ each.' (Wikipedia)
figure: 440 dead (60 under 20); manager fined £24; 'lives at 1/1¼ each'
source: Wikipedia, 'Senghenydd colliery disaster'

oneLiner: Gawber pit, Yorkshire, 1842 — Sarah Gooder, 8, a 'trapper,' sat alone in the dark opening a mine door: 'I'm scared.' (UK Royal Commission on Children's Employment)
source: The Victorian Web (Ashley's Mines Commission testimony)

oneLiner: Yorkshire, 1842 — Patience Kershaw, 17, hurried coal corves 'a mile and more' underground, beaten on the back when too slow. (UK Royal Commission on Children's Employment)
source: The Victorian Web (Ashley's Mines Commission testimony)

oneLiner: Scotland, 1842 — Isabella Read, 12, a coal-bearer, carried over 1 cwt on her back, stooping and creeping through water to the calves. (UK Royal Commission on Children's Employment)
source: The Victorian Web (Ashley's Mines Commission testimony)

oneLiner: Britain, May 1842 — the Royal Commission found children as young as 5 or 6 working underground 11-12 hrs/day; the Act then banned women and boys under 10. (Mines & Collieries Act 1842)
company: Royal Commission report / Mines and Collieries Act 1842
source: Wikipedia: Mines and Collieries Act 1842

oneLiner: Silkstone, Yorkshire, 4 July 1838 — 26 children aged 7-17 drowned fleeing the flooded Huskar Pit; the outcry led to the 1842 ban on child mine labour. (Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia: Huskar Pit

oneLiner: Barnsley, 12 Dec 1866 — firedamp explosions at the Oaks Colliery killed 361+ men and boys (research lists 383, incl. 91 children); 27 rescuers died next day. (Wikipedia)
place: Oaks Colliery, Hoyle Mill, Barnsley, Yorkshire
figure: 361 official; 383 named incl. 91 children; 27 rescuers killed
source: Discover Dearne research; Wikipedia: Oaks explosion

oneLiner: New Hartley, Northumberland, 16 Jan 1862 — a broken pump beam blocked the single shaft; 204 men and boys suffocated, forcing the law that mines need two exits. (Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia: Hartley Colliery disaster

oneLiner: Westhoughton, Lancashire, 21 Dec 1910 — a gas-and-dust explosion at the Pretoria Pit killed 344 men and boys; one family lost 7 members. (Hulton Colliery Co.; Wikipedia)
place: Pretoria Pit, Over Hulton, Westhoughton, Lancashire
source: Wikipedia: Pretoria Pit disaster

oneLiner: Felling, Gateshead, 25 May 1812 — a colliery explosion killed 92, including boys of 8, 10 and 12; the deaths spurred the invention of the Davy safety lamp. (Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia: Felling mine disasters

oneLiner: Fulbourn, Cambridge, Feb 1875 — George Brewster, 11, was sent up an asylum chimney and died; his master got 6 months' hard labour and Parliament finally banned climbing boys. (Cambridge PPF)
company: Master sweep William Wyer / Chimney Sweepers Act 1875
source: Cambridge Past, Present & Future (George Brewster)

oneLiner: London, 1775 — surgeon Percivall Pott traced 'soot-wart' scrotal cancer in chimney sweeps to climbing boys' soot exposure: the first occupational cancer ever identified. (Britannica)
figure: first occupational cancer; boys from age ~4
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Percivall Pott

oneLiner: Pennsylvania anthracite fields, c.1900-1911 — 'breaker boys' as young as 8 hand-picked slate ~10 hrs/day, 6 days/week, for roughly 70-80 cents; Lewis Hine photographed them for the NCLC. (PA Heritage; Yale)
company: Pennsylvania anthracite collieries / National Child Labor Committee (Lewis Hine)
source: Pennsylvania Heritage Magazine; Yale Energy History

oneLiner: Britain, 1879 — a Victorian 'maid-of-all-work' earned just £6-£15 a year, the lowest household wage. (Dickens's Dictionary of London)
company: Dickens's Dictionary of London (1879), Charles Dickens Jr.
source: Dickens's Dictionary of London (1879), via victorianlondon.org

oneLiner: Britain, c.1880s — the maid-of-all-work toiled 14-16 hours a day at the most menial chores, the era's hardest servant post. (Wojtczak; Victorian Web)
company: Helena Wojtczak, English Social History of Hastings & St Leonards
source: Helena Wojtczak, via The Victorian Web

oneLiner: Britain, 1873 — a housemaid worked 6am-10pm, ~80 hours a week versus 56 for a factory worker, with no union to protect her. (J. Burnett; Victorian Web)
company: John Burnett, The Annals of Labour (1974)
source: John Burnett / George P. Landow, The Victorian Web

oneLiner: Britain, 1851 — over a million domestic servants, mostly women: the second-largest occupation after agriculture, 'mute and forgotten.' (1851 Census; Burnett)
company: 1851 Census of Great Britain; Burnett, The Annals of Labour
source: 1851 Census scholarship; Burnett via Victorian Web

oneLiner: London, 1860 — maid Hannah Cullwick logged her own labor: boots cleaned by the hundred, 16-hour days, bed at 11. (Diaries of Hannah Cullwick)
source: The Diaries of Hannah Cullwick; Wikipedia

oneLiner: Britain, 1874 — 'a servant's work is never done... even her sleep is not sacred,' wrote Eliza Lynn Linton in The Cornhill Magazine. (On the Side of the Maids)
figure: no fixed hours; on call always
company: Eliza Lynn Linton, 'On the Side of the Maids', Cornhill Magazine vol.29
source: Cornhill Magazine (1874), via The Victorian Web

oneLiner: Norfolk, 1920 — a 14-year-old 'tweeny' rose at 6am, retired at 10pm, blackleading ranges and scrubbing floors for £1 a month. (Within Living Memory, Norfolk WI)
source: Within Living Memory (Norfolk WI, 1971), via Stoke Ferry & District History Group

oneLiner: England, 1850-1930 — laundresses ironed till 2am over four-day wash cycles; the Royal Commission called them 'the most independent people on earth' — not as praise. (Malcolmson)
company: Royal Commission on Labour; P. Malcolmson, English Laundresses (1986)
source: Patricia Malcolmson, English Laundresses: A Social History 1850-1930

oneLiner: Brighton, c.1900 — laundresses worked up to 14 hrs/day, 60/week amid steam, unguarded mangles and lye, suffering burns and ulcers; girls under 15 paid less for the same work. (Brighton Women's History Group)
source: Brighton & Hove Women's History Group

oneLiner: Atlanta, 1881 — 3,000 Black washerwomen of the Washing Society struck for $1 per 12 lbs of wash, facing arrests and fines, and won. (1881 Atlanta Washerwomen Strike)
company: The Washing Society; Atlanta City Council
source: 1881 Atlanta Washerwomen Strike, Wikipedia; AFL-CIO labor history

oneLiner: Ireland, 1922-1996 — at least 10,000 girls and women were confined in Magdalene Laundries, washing commercial loads for no pay. (McAleese Report, 2013)
company: Sisters of Mercy / Good Shepherd & others; McAleese Report (2013)
source: Justice for Magdalenes Research; McAleese Report (Irish govt, Feb 2013)

oneLiner: England, 1890 — 'over eight thousand of these little slaveys come from workhouse schools, placed out by the guardians at thirteen or fourteen' as domestic servants. (The Hospital, 6 Sept 1890)
company: Boards of Guardians, Poor Law system
source: 'Working Women in Large Towns: IX. Domestic Servants,' The Hospital (London)

oneLiner: Mauritius, 1834 — Britain launched Indian indenture to cheaply replace freed slaves; ~1.6M 'coolies' shipped to 19 colonies by 1917. (Indian indenture system; Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia, 'Indian indenture system'

oneLiner: British colonies, 1834-1917 — historian Hugh Tinker titled his study 'A New System of Slavery'; early voyages killed over 17% from cholera, dysentery & overcrowding. (Wikipedia; Tinker 1974)
role: Indian indentured labourer aboard emigrant ships
source: Hugh Tinker, 'A New System of Slavery' (1974); Wikipedia, 'Indian indenture system'

oneLiner: British Guiana & Trinidad, 1838+ — indentured men earned ~1 shilling/day (women ~9d) cutting cane 10-12 hrs; an 1864 Demerara ordinance jailed workers for absence/breach of contract. (Leicester MNS)
source: 'Immigration and Incarceration in Post-Emancipation British Guiana,' Univ. of Leicester (mnsguyana)

oneLiner: Fiji, 1879-1916 — ~60,500 Indian 'girmityas' cut cane for Australia's CSR Co.; in 1910 missionary J.W. Burton reported they 'frankly call it narak (hell)' and saw it as worse than slavery.
source: J.W. Burton, 'The Fiji of To-day' (1910), via Wikipedia 'Indo-Fijians'

oneLiner: Cuba, 1847-1874 — of 142,422 Chinese shipped as 'coolies' to sugar estates, ~1 in 10 died at sea; the 1874 Cuba Commission found 8 in 10 taken 'by force or fraud.' (US State Dept / FRUS)
role: Chinese contract 'coolie' on Cuban sugar plantations
figure: 142,422 shipped; ~1 in 10 died at sea; ~80% taken by force/fraud
source: US Dept. of State, Office of the Historian, FRUS 1875 (Cuba Commission Report)

oneLiner: Peru, c.1849-1874 — Chinese 'coolies' dug bird-dung (guano) under the lash on the Chincha Is.; by 1860 not one of the 4,000 brought since the trade began had survived. (Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia, 'Chincha Islands'

oneLiner: Macao to Havana, 1847-1874 — Chinese 'coolie' ships were called 'floating coffins'; ~16,400 of ~140,000 bound for Cuba died at sea, many vessels former African slave ships. (Katz Fine Manuscripts)
role: Chinese 'coolie' in the Pacific passage to the Americas
source: Jessica Katz, 'Macao to Havana and Beyond: The Chinese-Cuban Coolie Trade,' Katz Fine Manuscripts

oneLiner: Congo Free State, 1885-1908 — Leopold II's rubber regime worked Congolese to death for quotas; Force Publique soldiers severed hands as proof of spent cartridges; ~10M dead (est.). (Wikipedia)
figure: 3-4 kg dried rubber per man per fortnight; ~10M dead (est.)
company: ABIR / Force Publique under Leopold II
source: Wikipedia, 'Atrocities in the Congo Free State' (Hochschild/Vansina record)

oneLiner: Kasai River, Congo, 1899 — missionary William Sheppard documented a chief drying 81 severed right hands, kept by the state as a body count for rubber enforcement. (Wikipedia)
role: Congolese rubber labourers under the severed-hands quota system
place: Kasai River region, Congo Free State
company: Leopold II's Congo Free State / Force Publique
source: Wikipedia, 'Atrocities in the Congo Free State' (William Sheppard's report)

oneLiner: Congo, 1904 — Roger Casement's British consular report confirmed mutilation & depopulation; a 1919 Belgian commission judged roughly half the population had perished. (Wikipedia)
role: Congolese forced rubber labourers (documented in official inquiry)
company: Leopold II's Congo Free State (Casement Report / Congo Reform Assoc.)
source: Wikipedia, 'Atrocities in the Congo Free State' (Casement Report; 1919 Belgian commission)

oneLiner: Putumayo, Amazon, 1910 — Casement found J.C. Arana's London-listed rubber co. ran 'not merely slavery but extermination'; up to 40,000 Huitoto & Bora died, scarred by the 'Mark of Arana.' (Wikipedia)
source: Wikipedia, 'Putumayo genocide' (Roger Casement's report)

oneLiner: Sierra Nevada, June 1867 — 3,000 Chinese railroad workers struck for $40/mo and a 10-hr day; the Central Pacific cut off their food to break them in a week. (Wikipedia)
figure: $31-35/mo vs $40 demanded; cut to 10-hr day demanded
source: Wikipedia, '1867 Chinese Labor Strike'

oneLiner: Queensland, 1863-1908 — ~55,000-62,500 Pacific Islanders ('Kanakas') were blackbirded onto sugar plantations by deception & kidnapping; about 15,000 died. (Wikipedia)
role: South Sea Islander ('Kanaka') indentured cane labourer
source: Wikipedia, 'Blackbirding'

oneLiner: Europe, 1770 — von Kempelen's chess 'automaton', the Mechanical Turk, hid a human inside; Amazon revived the name for AI ghost work. (Crawford, 'Atlas of AI'; IEEE Spectrum)
role: hidden human chess operator concealed inside a fake 'thinking machine'
figure: built 1770; toured ~84 years as a hoax automaton
company: The Mechanical Turk (Wolfgang von Kempelen); namesake of Amazon Mechanical Turk
source: Oscar Schwartz, IEEE Spectrum; Crawford, 'Atlas of AI'

oneLiner: Ivan Illich named it 'shadow work' (1980): unpaid toil — housework, commuting, form-filling — that industrial society demands so wage labor can exist. (Philosophica 26)
role: philosopher / social critic naming unpaid labor
source: Illich, 'Shadow-Work,' Philosophica 26 (1980); nurturedevelopment.org PDF

oneLiner: Illich: shadow work is 'a kind of forced labor or industrial serfdom' — unpaid, compulsory, the necessary complement to the family wage. (Shadow Work, Marion Boyars, 1981)
role: theory of disowned/unpaid labor under industrialism
company: Ivan Illich, 'Shadow Work,' Marion Boyars Publishers
source: The Anarchist Library (full text of Illich, Shadow Work)

oneLiner: Margaret Benston, 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation' (Monthly Review, Sept 1969) — housework is socially necessary production left outside the wage. (Monthly Review)
role: precursor: domestic labor as production for use, not 'real work'
source: Monthly Review archives

oneLiner: Padua, 1972 — Dalla Costa, Federici, James & Galtier found the International Feminist Collective, launching the Wages for Housework campaign. (Wikipedia)
role: feminist organizers demanding pay for unwaged domestic labor
company: International Feminist Collective / International Wages for Housework Campaign
source: Wikipedia, 'Wages for housework'

oneLiner: Manchester, March 1972 — Selma James first puts Wages for Housework to the UK Women's Liberation conference; it is voted down and rejected for years after. (LSE History)
role: feminist organizer; demand for a wage for housework
company: Selma James, 'Women, the Unions and Work' (1972)
source: LSE History blog; Global Women's Strike

oneLiner: Dalla Costa & James, 'The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community' (1972) — recast housework as reproductive labor capitalism needs but renders invisible. (libcom)
role: Marxist-feminist theory of invisible reproductive labor
company: Mariarosa Dalla Costa & Selma James, Falling Wall Press
source: libcom.org full text; Wikipedia, 'Wages for housework'

oneLiner: 'They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work.' — Silvia Federici, Wages Against Housework (1975), the pamphlet that named housework as work. (caringlabor archive)
role: feminist theorist; wage demand as refusal of unpaid care
place: Bristol/New York (Power of Women Collective & Falling Wall Press)
source: caring labor: an archive (full pamphlet text)

oneLiner: Federici, Caliban and the Witch (2004): capitalism's rise required a 'war against women' — the witch-hunts that disciplined unpaid reproductive labor. (Wikipedia)
role: historian of primitive accumulation & disowned women's labor
company: Silvia Federici, 'Caliban and the Witch,' Autonomedia
source: Wikipedia, 'Caliban and the Witch'

oneLiner: Social reproduction theory: the unpaid work that makes workers — cooking, care, childrearing — is what capitalism runs on yet refuses to count. (Radical Philosophy, Federici)
role: Marxist-feminist frame for unwaged social reproduction
company: Silvia Federici, 'Social reproduction theory: History, issues and present challenges'
source: Radical Philosophy (2.04, 2019)
